notes.title: Why networks exist: origins and business need
notes.caption: Networks did not start with computers. A deal is only as fast as the information behind it.
keys: Networks did not start with computers — they started with people signalling, long before any device.
Human, mechanical, then electronic signalling were used by people, communities, and companies to send a message farther and faster.
Business = exchange of information: a deal is only as fast as the information behind it.

notes.title: Naming, addressing and regulation: directory to DNS
notes.caption: Before DNS, the directory was a telephone book run by government. Names are delegated, addresses allocated by region.
keys: Before DNS, the directory was a telephone book run by government, used by telecom companies, businesses, and people.
ICANN, RIRs, and IP blocks: names are delegated hierarchically and addresses allocated by region, so networks can find each other.
FCC, TRAI, IETF, IEEE, and 3GPP regulate telecom companies, spectrum, and standards.

notes.title: Hardware supply and the NIC endpoint
notes.caption: Silicon becomes a chip, a chip becomes a vendor's device, and that device reaches a customer through the NIC.
keys: Silicon becomes a chip, and a chip becomes a vendor's device that a telecom company or business can buy and use.
Intel, Broadcom, and Nvidia supply hardware controlled by software, for cloud, OEMs, telcos, and government labs.
That device only reaches a customer through the NIC endpoint, on PCI, with a driver and operating system.

notes.title: The NIC and kernel stack, plus out-of-band management
notes.caption: Two lanes that must not be confused: the data lane and the management lane.
keys: A customer's traffic goes through the NIC interface, driver, kernel stack, net device, and TCP/IP.
Two lanes must not be confused: the data lane carries traffic, the management lane manages the device, even when it is down.
Out-of-band to BMC, then CLI, web, or API, lets a company manage a device while its data lane is down, so trading can resume faster and market trust is kept.

notes.title: Building, operating and approving a product
notes.caption: A product closes the loop: built, tested, sold, bought from vendors, gated by approval.
keys: A product is built by engineering and operations, tested, sold to customers, and bought through vendors who buy silicon.
FCC approval is the gate: equipment certification for routers and phones, and a broadband speed report, before market entry.
That gate depends on every card before it — origins, naming, hardware, and the NIC stack.
